podcast.title: Dislike for Synthesized "Bandstand Boogie" Theme (1974)
podcast.body: Barry Manilow, who grew up watching American Bandstand and fondly remembered Les Elgart's original theme, strongly disliked the 1974 synthesized update by Mike Kerb. He found the Moog synthesizer version unrecognizable and uninspiring, which prompted him to collaborate with Bruce Sussman to write new lyrics for the original tune. "The most crushing blow came when I heard their theme. Their theme is played on a moog synthesizer now."

podcast.title: Robert Hilburn's Criticism (1978)
podcast.body: In a 1978 review of Manilow's Greek Theater concert in Los Angeles, critic Robert Hilburn predictably dismissed the performance as "plain and bland." However, Hilburn also suggested that Manilow "was the beneficiary of the public's renewed fondness for simple, unprobing artists." "Robert Hillburn wrote a review of the opening night of a seven-night run of Manelow concerts at the Greek theater in Los Angeles in 1978, and predictably said it was plain and bland and blah, blah, blah, blah."

podcast.title: Impact on UK Musicians Union (1982)
podcast.body: Barry Manilow's decision to replace his orchestra with synthesizers during his tours sparked outrage within the UK Musicians Union in 1982. This move was a primary catalyst for the union to pass a motion demanding that synthesizers be banned, viewing them as a threat to musicians' livelihoods. "The problem was this guy. In 1982, Barry Manolo was a huge star."

podcast.title: Private Life and Coming Out (2014)
podcast.body: Barry Manilow maintained a deeply private personal life throughout much of his career. In 2014, at the age of 73, he publicly came out and announced his marriage to his manager, a man with whom he had been together since 1978. He explained his delay in coming out was due to not wanting to disappoint his fans. "So much so, that a lot of people were surprised when in 2014 at the age of 73, he came out and announced that he was married to his manager, a man, and they had been together since 1978."

podcast.title: Anti-Vax Protest Deterrence (2022)
podcast.body: In early 2022, authorities in New Zealand used Barry Manilow's greatest hits, mixed with "Macarena" on a 15-minute loop, to help break up an anti-vax protest. The tactic was described as working great. "In New Zealand, in early 2022, authorities helped break up an anti-vax protest by blasting the crowd with a mix of Barry Manelow's greatest hits and the Macarena on a 15 minute loop."

podcast.title: Catalyst for Musicians Union Backlash Against Synths
podcast.body: Barry Manilow became the "last straw" for the UK Musicians Union on May 23, 1982, prompting their public grievances against synthesizers. Previously touring with a string section, he replaced his orchestra with just a couple of synth players in 1981, leading to job losses for traditional musicians and escalating calls for a ban on synthesizers. "The last straw wasn't craftwork, or OMD, or Durand Durand, but very Manolo, one of the biggest mainstream artists at that time. In the past, Manolo had gone on tour with a string section, providing musicians with a solid living. But in 1981, he dumped the orchestra and toured with just a couple of synth players. That had to stop."

podcast.title: Concert Medleys of Jingles
podcast.body: In a testament to his unique career path, Barry Manilow openly acknowledges and celebrates his years in advertising by performing medleys of his famous jingles during his concerts. These medleys often feature his work for brands like Stridex, KFC, and State Farm. "Manila not only doesn't shy away from his years of advertising work, in concert, he plays medley's of his jingles for the likes of Stridex, KFC, and State Farm."

podcast.title: Conventional Career Post-Continental Baths
podcast.body: Despite performing shirtless at the Continental Baths in New York, surrounded by "nearly naked gay men," Manilow went on to have a notably conventional career, which seemed to be a deliberate choice. "it is interesting that a guy who performed shirtless at the continental baths in New York surrounded by nearly naked gay men ended up with such a conventional career. That seemed to be by design."

podcast.title: Early Career and Public Scrutiny
podcast.body: Barry Manilow was a frequent target of ridicule in the 1970s and 80s. Before achieving stardom, he worked accompanying Bette Midler in New York bathhouses. Dick Clark, while initially underestimating Manilow's star potential based on his looks and voice, recognized his talent for arranging and producing emotionally resonant songs. John Wasserman of the San Francisco Chronicle once skeptically questioned his star aspirations. "It was very fashionable to make fun of Barry Manelow in the 70s and in the 80s."

podcast.title: Early Career as Jingle Writer
podcast.body: Before his pop success, Barry Manilow was a jazz-influenced jingle writer, creating memorable tunes such as the Band-Aid commercial jingle (which featured Terry Garr and John Travolta), the State Farm jingle, and "You Deserve a Break Today" for McDonald's. His skill in writing catchy hooks for commercials was later replicated in his pop songs. "Manelow was a jazz-impluenced jingle writer, so maybe this was your first exposure to his work. There you have it. Terry Gar and John Travolta are both in that band-aid commercial house 70s. That Barry Manelow also wrote the state farm jingle. He wrote, you deserve a break today for McDonald's."

podcast.title: Fan Defense of Music's Emotional Impact
podcast.body: Barry W. Crown of Sherman Oaks wrote to Hilburn, defending Manilow by arguing that an artist "does not have to be, quote, heavy to conjure up thoughts and emotions," suggesting that Manilow's music resonated deeply with listeners, perhaps indicating a public weariness with the "commentary invite of Bob Dylan, etc." "An artist does not have to be, quote, heavy to conjure up thoughts and emotions. Manelow reaches into all of us, and maybe this supposed commentary invite of Bob Dylan, etc., is something we have grown tired of or have outgrown. Moods of people change, and the Dylan era represents years past."

podcast.title: Jingle Writer and Singer
podcast.body: Barry Manilow was not only a jingle singer but also a prolific writer of multiple jingles, several of which became widely recognized "earworms." His compositions include memorable tunes for brands such as Band-Aid, Stridex, KFC, and State Farm. "He was not just a jinglesinger. He wrote multiple jingles. And I'll bet you know several of them because they're earworms."

podcast.title: Touring Orchestra Replacement (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, during a severe recession, Barry Manilow, a huge star, faced financial pressure to cut touring expenses. Consequently, he replaced his full orchestra—including violinists, cellists, and brass sections—with "a couple of guys with synthesizers," whose keyboards could emulate all the necessary orchestral sounds. "Manolo couldn't afford to take a full orchestra with him on tour anymore. So all those musicians, violinists, cellists, brass sections, and so on, were replaced by a couple of guys with synthesizers."
